country_overview: The United States Federal Reserve System (the Federal Reserve) is the central bank and sets monetary policy, while U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) administer cross-border currency reporting. The United States operates a highly open foreign-exchange framework: no general exchange controls or capital controls on current account and capital account movement were identified in the reviewed federal sources or accessible IMF materials, subject to carve-outs for sanctions (OFAC), AML/Bank Secrecy Act reporting, tax, and sector-specific requirements. The US dollar is the world's primary reserve currency.

summary.traveler: Travelers may carry unlimited US dollars or foreign currency, but any person transporting more than USD 10,000 in aggregate — cash or monetary instruments — into or out of the United States must file a Currency and Monetary Instrument Report (FinCEN Form 105) with CBP at the border. Amounts of USD 10,000 or less require no declaration.
summary.business: Businesses and individuals can generally hold, transfer, convert, and repatriate foreign currency through authorised institutions. No general exchange-control or prior-approval regime was identified in the reviewed sources, subject to sanctions, AML reporting, tax, and sector-specific requirements.

rules.bring_foreign_currency_in: Foreign currency and US dollars may be imported without limit or prohibition. Any person bringing more than USD 10,000 in aggregate (cash or monetary instruments) into the United States must file FinCEN Form 105 (CMIR) with a CBP officer at the port of entry.
rules.take_foreign_currency_out: US dollars and foreign currency may be exported without limit. Any person taking more than USD 10,000 in aggregate (cash or monetary instruments) out of the United States must file FinCEN Form 105 (CMIR) with CBP before departure; non-residents may freely re-export funds they lawfully brought in.
rules.cash_declaration_threshold: The reporting threshold is USD 10,000. Under 31 U.S.C. 5316 and 31 CFR 1010.340, transporting an aggregate amount exceeding that figure across the US border triggers a mandatory Currency and Monetary Instrument Report (FinCEN Form 105) to CBP. This traveler border report is distinct from Bank Secrecy Act filings by financial institutions — Currency Transaction Reports (CTR) and Suspicious Activity Reports (SAR) — and from Foreign Bank Account Reports (FBAR); none of those is a traveler declaration.
rules.resident_holding_rules: No general prior-approval or exchange-control requirement barring US residents from holding or maintaining foreign-currency accounts with authorised institutions was identified in the reviewed federal sources or accessible IMF materials. Account access remains subject to sanctions screening, AML/KYC and reporting obligations, tax reporting, and institution-level requirements.
rules.non_resident_rules: For non-residents, no general prior-approval or exchange-control barrier to opening or operating accounts or transferring funds was identified in the reviewed sources. Onboarding and transfers remain subject to sanctions screening, AML/KYC, information-reporting and withholding rules, and each institution's own requirements.
rules.business_invoicing_settlement: Business transactions may be invoiced and settled in US dollars or foreign currency. No general exchange-control approval regime for cross-border commercial payments or repatriation was identified in the reviewed sources, subject to sanctions, AML reporting, tax, and sector-specific requirements.
rules.exchange_controls: No general exchange-control or prior-approval regime governing the holding, conversion, or cross-border movement of currency was identified in the reviewed federal sources or accessible IMF materials; the United States is an IMF member under Article IV surveillance. Specific carve-outs apply: OFAC-administered economic sanctions, Bank Secrecy Act / AML reporting, tax reporting, and sector or prudential rules.
rules.banking_conversion_practicality: In practice, foreign-exchange conversion and transfers are widely available through banks, licensed money-services businesses, and ATMs across the United States. Access is subject to each institution's AML/KYC and sanctions-screening procedures and to applicable reporting.

disclaimer: This page provides general informational reference only. Foreign-exchange rules in the United States are subject to change, and transaction-specific requirements may depend on residency status, documentation, amount, and the applicable Federal Reserve / CBP / FinCEN framework. This is not legal, regulatory, tax, financial, or compliance advice. Always verify current rules directly with US Customs and Border Protection, the Federal Reserve, or a qualified professional before making any financial or travel decisions.
